label: copy-phase input token z
explanation: Fires when the token fed back as input during the copy phase is z (the model just emitted z). Every copy-phase z input fires it (dev precision 1.0, recall 0.96, mass recall 0.99). It does not fire on z in the original phase (only a few very weak activations there) or on other tokens, apart from rare weak (~0.1-0.15) activations on x/f/m. In the examples, magnitude is lower when the z is the first copy input, right after <DEL> (orig(0) = z, about 0.4-0.6), and when it directly follows another z (about 0.8 vs 0.95). It is highest for a z that follows a non-z token in the middle of the copy.

issues: Core predicate holds. Test precision is 1.0, recall 0.963, F1 0.981 and mass recall 0.993, with 0 false positives on the test split. Copy-phase in_tok carries 99.6% of the activation mass.
Original-phase z barely fires: (phase==0)&(in_tok==z) has precision 0.016 and mass recall 0.004. So 'only a few very weak activations there' is correct.

Missed activations are weak and scattered: 3555 test steps holding 0.7% of the mass, mostly in the lowest quartile. There are two small patterns. One is weak firing (about 0.1-0.2) on an original-phase z. The other is the copy-phase input just before a z input, i.e. when out_tok==z, which has precision 0.019 and mass 0.003. Neither is big enough to justify a new predicate.

The magnitude claim is partly wrong. A z that follows another z is not weaker: (phase==2)&(in_tok==z)&(prev_tok==z) has mass/count ratio about 1.045, slightly above the feature average, not about 0.8 vs 0.95 as claimed. The first copy input (recall_idx==1) is only marginally weaker in aggregate (ratio about 0.98). The 0.4-0.6 values in the examples appear to be relative to the max. These are minor descriptive details taken from a few examples and do not affect the label.
